safetyNote: Do not eat Lactarius turpis (syn. L. necator), even after boiling or pickling. DGfM lists gastrointestinal poisoning and a suspected mutagenic or carcinogenic risk. A laboratory study found the mutagenic compound necatorin in fresh mushrooms and found that blanching reduced, but did not eliminate, its concentration. This is evidence of hazard, not a measured human cancer risk. Its historical food use does not establish safety; seek poison-centre advice after ingestion or symptoms.

sections.title: Dark olive, sticky cap
sections.text: The robust cap is commonly about 5–15 cm, occasionally larger. It begins convex with a long-inrolled margin, then flattens and becomes depressed or funnel-shaped. Colour is olive-green to deep olive-brown, sometimes almost black in old or injured specimens, often a little paler yellow-olive at the edge. The cap is felted when young but soon smoother, with dark embedded fibres; in wet weather it becomes slimy or sticky. It is usually not clearly zoned.

sections.title: Pale gills that brown
sections.text: Close, low cream gills are often forked near the stem and run shortly down it. Damaged gills turn sepia to dark brown, while abundant white latex may dry grey-green or olive-brown. The shortish, robust stem is usually paler dirty olive than the cap, sometimes with shallow pits; it becomes hollow in old specimens. Firm pale flesh browns with injury and age. The latex and flesh are intensely acrid, but tasting a suspected poisonous mushroom is unnecessary and unsafe.

sections.title: Birch and spruce woods
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal mushroom occurs with birch and spruce, frequently on acidic soil, from summer into late autumn. In Britain it is often found with birch at wet woodland edges. The cap's wet sliminess, dark olive tones, browning gills, white latex and host tree should be checked together. Other olive milkcaps can be smaller and paler, so a single photograph is insufficient for confident identification.

sections.title: Necatorin and health evidence
sections.text: The older name L. necator appears in toxicological studies. Suortti measured necatorin in fresh specimens and observed that blanching left roughly one quarter of the initial concentration; this result does not establish a safe cooking method. DGfM records a gastrointestinal syndrome and labels cancer-causing or mutagenic effects as suspected, rather than proven human outcomes. Despite traditional processing and use as a seasoning in some regions, the Czech Mycological Society advises against collecting it for food.

traits: Large dark olive-green to nearly blackish cap, often 5–15 cm, depressed with age and sticky when wet
Young long-inrolled, initially felted margin; cap usually lacks clear concentric zones
Close cream gills, shortly decurrent, browning strongly when injured
Short stout dirty-olive stem, sometimes shallowly pitted and hollowing when old
Abundant white, intensely acrid latex, drying grey-green or olive-brown; pale flesh browns
Birch and spruce associate on often acidic soils, summer to late autumn
